```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Did participants enjoy the community course? How did their assessment scores
compare across centres? tidystata helps answer these first questions inside a
tidyverse workflow: start with a tibble, inspect it, prepare columns with
`mutate()`, and pass results to the next step with `|>`.

Install tidystata using the instructions on the
[package homepage](https://socimh.github.io/tidystata/). We attach dplyr and
tibble individually; the full tidyverse package is not required.

## Meet the survey

Twelve participants attended courses at Riverside and Hilltop. Each answered
a yes/no satisfaction question and two assessment items. Some answers are missing,
and income arrived as text.

```{r survey, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied, ~income_text, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,200",           2,       4,
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,500",           4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside", "No",      "",               NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside", NA,        "-99",             6,       8,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",     "2,200",           8,      10,
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,800",           4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",      "1,400",           3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,100",           5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",      "2,600",           7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     NA,                9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,300",          NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",   NA,        "1,700",           6,       8
)

survey |> codebook()
```

There are six participants per centre. The codebook shows which columns contain
text, how many values are observed, and where the gaps are. An identifier is
numeric too, but we will select assessment items deliberately when summarising.

## Prepare measurements with `mutate()`

The survey form uses `-99` for an undisclosed income. Read the numeric text, turn
that code into `NA`, and calculate an average across the two assessment items.

```{r prepare}
prepared <- survey |>
  mutate(
    income = destring(income_text) |> mvdecode(-99),
    score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)),
    answered = row_non_miss(pick(score1, score2))
  )

prepared |> select(id, income, score, answered)
```

Participant 2 has one assessment answer, so the average uses that answer.
Participant 3 has none: the average is `NA` and `answered` is zero.
`destring()` also reads the thousands separators; blank text becomes missing.

## Count responses

How many participants were satisfied?

```{r count}
prepared |> tab(satisfied)
```

Seven said yes. That is 58.3% of all twelve participants, or 70% of the ten
who answered. The `percent` and `valid` columns make both denominators visible.
The two missing answers remain a category.

Results are tibbles here, so ordinary dplyr verbs can answer a follow-up question:

```{r reuse-counts}
prepared |>
  tab(satisfied, .by = centre) |>
  filter(satisfied == "Yes") |>
  select(centre, n, valid)
```

## Compare measurements

Now compare the assessment average across centres.

```{r summarise}
prepared |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd"))
```

Each mean uses the observed scores in that centre. The returned table is ready
for another pipeline; no results need to be copied out of console output.
Use `tabstat()` when a compact table of means is enough.
